# Peach

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="peach-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="peach-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="peach-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Peach in the HMI library has 283 reported results for lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, uranium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, Ba and Mo from 21 sources.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jane Houlihan, Charlotte Brody · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food">What&#39;s in My Baby&#39;s Food? <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-peach" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-peach-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of peach, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>151</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>Houlihan et al. 2019</td><td>1</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024</td><td>5</td><td>33%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for peach, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>3 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li><li><a href="../sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food" class="internal" data-slug="sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food" data-no-cite-meta>Houlihan et al. 2019</a></li><li><a href="../sources/fda2024-toxic-elements-baby-food-compliance-2009-2024" class="internal" data-slug="sources/fda2024-toxic-elements-baby-food-compliance-2009-2024" data-no-cite-meta>U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, peach, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (2.4 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (720 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (1 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (60 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

In one study, lead across 6 groups of peach ranged from 55.5 µg/kg (Toronto 1988) to 196 µg/kg (Montreal 1988); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dabeka RW, McKenzie AD · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Survey of Lead, Cadmium, Fluoride, Nickel, and Cobalt in Food Composites and Estimation of Dietary Intakes of These Elements by Canadians in 1986-1988</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of AOAC International</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

## Processing, cooking and preparation

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>

Processed or prepared forms were compared only with unprocessed peach in the same study and group. Peach, canned (5 city composites) had lead higher at 143 µg/kg, against 14.8 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (peach, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dabeka RW, McKenzie AD · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Survey of Lead, Cadmium, Fluoride, Nickel, and Cobalt in Food Composites and Estimation of Dietary Intakes of These Elements by Canadians in 1986-1988</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of AOAC International</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, peach, juice (PAHO) had lead higher at 16.6 µg/kg, against 2.4 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (peach, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A third study found that peach, peel or outer layer (local market, Quetta; brought from Sawat; June-July 2019) had lead lower at 135 µg/kg, against 824 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (peach, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/nisa2020-quetta-market-fruits-vegetables-metals|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Nisa KU, Samiullah, Khan N, Attiq-ur-Rehman · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/nisa2020-quetta-market-fruits-vegetables-metals">Detection of Heavy metals in Fruits and Vegetables available in the Market of Quetta city</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Al-Nahrain Journal of Science 23(1):47-56</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/nisa2020-quetta-market-fruits-vegetables-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.

Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Peach FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-peach" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-peach" data-question="What heavy metals are found in peach?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in peach?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, uranium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, Ba and Mo in peach, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jane Houlihan, Charlotte Brody · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food">What&#39;s in My Baby&#39;s Food? A National Investigation Finds 95 Percent of Baby Foods Tested Contain Toxic Chemicals That Lower Babies&#39; IQ, Including Arsenic and Lead</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Healthy Babies Bright Futures</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/houlihan2019-hbbf-whats-in-baby-food">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/lee2023-south-korea-fresh-fruits-seven-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Lee J, Hwang I, Park YS, Lee DY · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/lee2023-south-korea-fresh-fruits-seven-metals">Occurrence and health risk assessment of antimony, arsenic, barium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, and lead in fresh fruits consumed in South Korea</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Biological Chemistry</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/lee2023-south-korea-fresh-fruits-seven-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO GEMS/Food submissions reported lead in peach, as sold from 2,188 results in 4 reporting regions, with subgroup medians from 2.4 to 720 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-peach" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-peach" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in peach?">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same peach.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dabeka RW, McKenzie AD · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Survey of Lead, Cadmium, Fluoride, Nickel, and Cobalt in Food Composites and Estimation of Dietary Intakes of These Elements by Canadians in 1986-1988</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of AOAC International</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Peach, canned (5 city composites) had lead higher at 143 µg/kg, against 14.8 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (peach, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dabeka RW, McKenzie AD · 1995</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Survey of Lead, Cadmium, Fluoride, Nickel, and Cobalt in Food Composites and Estimation of Dietary Intakes of These Elements by Canadians in 1986-1988</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of AOAC International</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dabeka1995-canadian-food-composites-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>
